# John 2 · The First Sign and the Cleansed Temple (KJV)
> Unit john-02 · John 2:1–25 · loop john-kjv-study v2.0 · DRAFT for human doctrine review

## 🧭 At a Glance
### 🧵 Golden Thread
At a village wedding and in the temple courts, Jesus shows that he himself is what Israel's water of purifying and Israel's temple were waiting for: he gives the good wine of the new age, and he is the true temple, destroyed and raised on the third day, so faith must rest on him and not on the show.

### 🌗 Life & Light Line
John 2 answers a feast that has run dry and a worship gone stale in ritual and trade with the Son who turns purifying water into the best wine and who is himself the living house of God. It exposes a faith that feeds on wonders while the heart stays closed, and it gives the light of a Lord who knows what is in man and still calls us to believe on him.

### 🎯 Objectives
- Explain from John 2:6–11 and John 2:19–21 how the wine and the temple both present Jesus as the fulfilment of Israel's purification and worship.
- Distinguish, from John 2:11 and John 2:23–25, faith that rests on Jesus himself from faith that feeds on signs, and name one mark of each.
- **Doing:** This week, bring one place where the wine has run out to Jesus in prayer, obey one plain word of his at once as the servants did (John 2:5–7), and tell one person what he did.

## 🏛️ Core Foundations
### ✝️ Christological Root
**Gospel Foundation:** The chapter turns on one thing Jesus did and one thing he said. At Cana he acted, and John tells us what the act meant: "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." (John 2:11) In the temple he spoke the saying that explains both scenes: "Jesus answered and said unto them, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." (John 2:19) John does not leave us guessing which temple he meant: "But he spake of the temple of his body." (John 2:21)

**The Bridge:** Both deeds say the same thing. The means Israel used to draw near to God, the water of purifying and the house of sacrifice, were signposts, and in Jesus the signposts have reached what they pointed to. The doctrine grounded here is Christ as the fulfilment of the ceremonial law and the true dwelling of God with men: the Word who "dwelt among us" (John 1:14) is the temple where God is met, and his resurrection on the third day is the sign that proves it.

**Canonical Echoes:** Jesus (John 2:19) → Promise (Malachi 3:1) → Doctrine (Colossians 2:9) → Life (1 Corinthians 6:19)

**What Gets Lost:** Taught without Christ at the center, Cana becomes a lesson about helping a host in trouble or about Mary's influence, and the temple scene becomes a lesson about church fundraising or about when anger is allowed. Both lose John's point: Jesus is the good wine and the true temple, and the chapter shows his glory, not our religion.

### ⚔️ Spiritual Warfare
**The Lie:** God can be approached on our terms: by ritual that manages him, by trade that profits from him, or by a faith that stays for the show and never hands over the heart.

**The Truth:** The Father's house is not a market, and the Son who cleanses it reads every heart: "make not my Father's house an house of merchandise" (John 2:16), "for he knew what was in man" (John 2:25).

**The Battleground:** The motives beneath worship: why we come to church, why we pray, what we are really asking Jesus for when we ask him for a sign.

**The Weapon:** The remembered word. The disciples overcame their confusion by Scripture recalled and the word of Jesus believed: "they believed the scripture, and the word which Jesus had said" (John 2:22). Scripture remembered, and the risen Christ trusted, overturns the tables in the heart.

### 🌱 Life Pathway
**The Theft:** In John 2 the thief steals in two quiet ways. At Cana, joy runs out at the very moment meant for joy, "They have no wine" (John 2:3), and the only water at hand is the water of ritual washing. At the temple, the place meant for prayer has become a place of profit, so that a Gentile who came to seek God in the outer court found cattle pens and coin tables instead. The theft is a religion that washes hands but cannot fill hearts, and a worship that has become busy and noisy but lifeless.

**The Source:** Jesus himself, who turns the water of purifying into wine better than the first, and who says of his own body, "in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19). His means in this chapter are his word, his sign, and his resurrection; he came "that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly" (John 10:10).

**The Channel:** The servants who filled the jars and carried the cup to the governor did not make the wine; they obeyed and they carried it. The believer is such a servant: filling jars at his word, and bearing what Christ has made to people who, like the governor, know not "whence it was" (John 2:9).

**The Abundance Guard:** Abundant life is fullness of life in Christ, not prosperity, ease, or freedom from suffering. The best wine at Cana is a sign of the new covenant, not a promise that our celebrations will never run short. The same Jesus who gave wine at a wedding was given vinegar on a cross (John 19:29), and the hour he spoke of at Cana was the hour of his death.

### 💡 Light Pathway
**The Darkness:** Two kinds. The first is worship turned into trade, where God's house becomes a place of merchandise and no one notices because everyone is busy. The second is subtler: a faith that believes when it sees wonders but keeps the heart shut, so that "Jesus did not commit himself unto them" (John 2:24).

**The Source:** Christ, who "knew all men" (John 2:24) and needs no one to testify of man. "For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts" (2 Corinthians 4:6), and he shines there in the face of the Son who sees us whole.

**The Lamp:** Scripture remembered and believed, as the disciples remembered it (John 2:17, 22); honest self-examination before the One who already knows; hidden motives confessed; the unfruitful works of darkness reproved, beginning in our own house (Ephesians 5:11); and good works that point people to the Father (Matthew 5:16).

**The Love Guard:** Light without love is glare. Jesus' zeal for his Father's house consumed him and led him to the cross (Psalm 69:9). Our zeal is never licence to shame others; we turn the lamp on our own heart before we carry it anywhere else.

### 🏺 Setting the Scene
Cana was a village in the hills of Galilee, a short walk from Nazareth; its exact site is still debated. A village wedding could last several days, and the bridegroom's family was expected to keep the guests supplied, so running out of wine was a public embarrassment. Six stone jars stood ready for the washings of Jewish purity custom (Mark 7:3–4). Stone was favoured for such vessels because, in the purity tradition later written down by the rabbis, stone did not take on ritual uncleanness the way clay did. Each held two or three firkins, the Greek measure of roughly nine gallons.

The scene then moves to Jerusalem at the first of the Passovers John names. Pilgrims came from far away and needed unblemished animals for sacrifice and the right coin for the half shekel given to the sanctuary (Exodus 30:13). Dealers and money changers had set up inside the temple precincts, most likely in the outer court, the only part of the temple a Gentile could enter. Herod the Great had begun a vast rebuilding of the temple, and the forty-six years the Jews mention in John 2:20 place this Passover around AD 27 or 28 on the usual reckoning.

Watch the narrator. John tells us things the people in the story do not know: the servants know where the wine came from, the governor does not, and the disciples understand the temple saying only after the resurrection.

### 🖍️ Read & Mark
**Marking key:** circle repeated words · underline commands · box names of God · double-underline promises

#### John 2:1–11 · The Wedding at Cana
**1** And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee; and the mother of Jesus was there:

**2** And both Jesus was called, and his disciples, to the marriage.

**3** And when they wanted wine, the mother of Jesus saith unto him, They have no wine.

**4** Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come.

**5** His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.

**6** And there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece.

**7** Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim.

**8** And he saith unto them, Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast. And they bare it.

**9** When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine, and knew not whence it was: (but the servants which drew the water knew;) the governor of the feast called the bridegroom,

**10** And saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now.

**11** This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him.

#### John 2:12–22 · The Temple at Passover
**12** After this he went down to Capernaum, he, and his mother, and his brethren, and his disciples: and they continued there not many days.

**13** And the Jews' passover was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem,

**14** And found in the temple those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting:

**15** And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables;

**16** And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise.

**17** And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.

**18** Then answered the Jews and said unto him, What sign shewest thou unto us, seeing that thou doest these things?

**19** Jesus answered and said unto them, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.

**20** Then said the Jews, Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days?

**21** But he spake of the temple of his body.

**22** When therefore he was risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this unto them; and they believed the scripture, and the word which Jesus had said.

#### John 2:23–25 · Many Believed, But
**23** Now when he was in Jerusalem at the passover, in the feast day, many believed in his name, when they saw the miracles which he did.

**24** But Jesus did not commit himself unto them, because he knew all men,

**25** And needed not that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man.

**View A:** 'Mine hour' in John 2:4 means the time for Jesus to begin acting publicly by signs. He declines to act at his mother's prompting, then acts in his own time the same day. Compare his answer when his brothers push him to show himself: "My time is not yet come" (John 7:6).

**View B:** 'Mine hour' means what the hour means everywhere else in John: the hour of his death, resurrection, and glory. Already at the first sign he has the cross in view, and the glory seen at Cana is a foretaste of the glory of that hour (John 12:23).

**Q11.** Which view does the text best support, and why? Weigh John 7:30, John 8:20, John 13:1, and John 17:1 before you answer.

### 👣 Case Study · Scripture in Action
Nehemiah came back to Jerusalem and found that Eliashib the priest had given Tobiah, an enemy of God's people, a great chamber in the courts of the house of God, the very room where the offerings and tithes were once stored (Nehemiah 13:4–7). Nehemiah writes that it grieved him sore, and he cast all Tobiah's household stuff out of the chamber, had the chambers cleansed, and brought the vessels of God's house back (Nehemiah 13:8–9). Yet the same chapter shows how quickly reform can slip: the Levites unpaid, the house of God forsaken (Nehemiah 13:10–11). Nehemiah's zeal was real and right, but he ends by asking God to remember him (Nehemiah 13:31); he could clean a room, but he could not make a new heart or become a better temple.

**Q12.** Nehemiah and Jesus both cleanse the house of God. What is the same in their zeal, and what does Jesus do in John 2:19–21 that Nehemiah never could?

### 🏙️ Modern Example
Marcus came to faith at a crowded healing service, and for a year he chased bigger experiences. When his mother's cancer returned and his prayers were not answered the way he asked, he told a friend he was done; God had stopped showing up. His friend opened John 2 with him and pointed out two kinds of believing in one chapter. The disciples saw the sign at Cana and 'believed on him', on the person. The crowd in Jerusalem believed because of the signs, and Jesus did not entrust himself to them. Then she showed him John 2:19–22: the one sign Jesus promised was his own death and resurrection, and the disciples understood it only after the cross. Marcus began reading John a chapter a day instead of looking for the next event. His mother's illness did not go away. But by spring he could say that he trusted Jesus because of who Jesus is, not because of what he had seen him do.

**Q13.** Where are you tempted to trust Jesus for what he shows you rather than for who he is, and what would it look like to believe "on him" (John 2:11) this week?

### 📜 Voices from Church History
The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), in its chapter on religious worship and the sabbath day, teaches two things this chapter helps to ground. First, the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is appointed by God himself and bounded by his revealed will, not devised by human imagination or convenience. Second, under the gospel no part of worship is now tied to any one place, or made more acceptable by the place where it is offered; God is to be worshipped everywhere in spirit and in truth. The divines drew the second point from John 4, but John 2 is where the move begins: the temple saying points away from a building to the risen body of Christ.

**Q14.** How does Jesus' cleansing of the temple support the conviction that God decides how he is to be worshipped, and where might your own worship have drifted toward what suits you rather than what honours him?

### ⛪ Doctrine in My Own Words
- **Theology Proper:** The Father is jealous for his house, and his worship is his to define, not ours to trade in (John 2:16).
- **Christology:** Jesus manifested his own glory in the sign at Cana, a glory that belongs to God alone (John 2:11).
- **Christology:** Jesus' risen body is the true temple, the place where God dwells with men and is met (John 2:21).
- **Christology:** Jesus knows every heart without being told, as only God does (John 2:25).
- **Anthropology & Sin:** The human heart can turn God's worship into trade and God's wonders into entertainment, and it can believe with the head while holding back the self (John 2:24).
- **Soteriology & Grace:** The new covenant wine replaces the water of purifying: cleansing and joy are given in Christ, not earned by ritual (John 2:10).
- **Christian Walk:** A disciple's rule of life is to do whatever Jesus says, trusting him before seeing the outcome (John 2:5).

### 👑 Christocentric & Humility · Level 4
Every problem in John 2 is answered in Jesus. The wine runs out, and he supplies better wine than the first. The water of purifying could wash hands and pots but never a conscience, and he is the one who by himself purged our sins (Hebrews 1:3). The temple has become a market, and he cleanses it and then names himself the temple. The Jews demand a sign, and he gives them the only sign that finally matters, his death and resurrection. The crowd's faith is shallow, and he knows every heart and still gives himself to those who believe on him. Every truth in the chapter is found in him as well: the glory of God, the purity God requires, the presence of God with his people, and the knowledge of God that searches us.

The chapter humbles us too. Mary steps back and points away from herself to her Son. The servants work unseen, and only they know where the wine came from. The bridegroom is praised for wine he never provided, and Jesus lets him take it; the Lord of glory is content that his first sign be known only to servants and disciples. Humility here is not self-hatred. It is getting out of the way so that Christ is seen.

**Humility Practices**
- Do one hidden act of service this week that no one will credit to you, like the servants who drew the water and said nothing (John 2:9).
- Before you ask God for anything today, pray Mary's words back to him as your own surrender: that you will do whatever he says (John 2:5).
- When someone else gets the praise for something God did through you, thank God quietly and let it go, remembering that Christ "must increase" (John 3:30).

**Q19.** In John 2:9–10 Jesus lets the bridegroom receive the praise for the good wine. What does that tell you about the kind of glory Jesus seeks, and how does it humble your own desire for credit?

### 💎 Memory Verse
"This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." (John 2:11)

**Why this verse:** It is John's own summary of the first sign: what Jesus did, where he did it, what it showed, and what it produced. It sets the pattern for the whole Gospel: signs manifest his glory, and glory seen calls for faith in him, which is exactly why John says he wrote (John 20:31).

- **Group question 2 · 7 min.** The wine and the temple both replace something old with something better (John 2:10, 21). What old things has Jesus replaced in your life, and what did he give instead? *Cue:* keep the answers personal and concrete; if the group drifts into criticizing other churches, bring it back to 'in my life'.
- **Group question 3 · 6 min.** Has your faith ever been more attached to what Jesus does than to who he is (John 2:23–25)? What moved you from one to the other? *Cue:* the leader answers first, briefly and honestly; no one is pressed to share.
