## 🟢 Tier 1 — Easy
### 📌 Core Concept
At a wedding party, the wine ran out, and Jesus turned big jars of washing water into the best wine anyone had tasted. He did it to show who he is: God's own Son, who brings a joy that does not run out. Then Jesus went to the temple in Jerusalem and chased out the people who were buying and selling there, because God's house is for meeting God, not for making money. When the leaders asked him to prove he had the right, he said something surprising: his own body is the real temple, and if they killed him, he would come back to life in three days. And that is exactly what happened.

### 📖 Key Verses
"His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." (John 2:5) Whatever Jesus tells us to do is the right thing to do.

"This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." (John 2:11) Jesus' miracles show how great he is, so that we will trust him.

"Jesus answered and said unto them, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." (John 2:19) Jesus knew he would die and rise again.

"And needed not that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man." (John 2:25) Nobody has to tell Jesus what we are like inside; he already knows.

### 🪞 Analogy
A road sign that says 'Lake, one mile' is a good sign, but nobody spreads a picnic blanket under the sign. When you reach the lake, you swim in the lake. The stone jars and the temple were like signs pointing to God. Jesus is the lake they were pointing to. Once he has come, we go to him.

### 🔎 Diagnostic Check
- When Jesus tells me something in the Bible, do I do it even if I don't understand why yet?
- Do I love Jesus for who he is, or mostly for what I hope he will give me?
- Do I ever do good things at church mostly so that people will notice me?
- Can I be glad when somebody else gets the thank-you for something good?
- Do I let Jesus see my whole heart, or do I try to hide parts of it from him?

### ✅ Action Step
This week, when a parent, a teacher, or the Bible tells you to do something good, do it the first time and do it all the way, the way the servants filled the jars right up to the top. Then say thank you to Jesus, because he is the one who makes good things out of ordinary water.

### 🌗 Life and Light, Simply
Jesus gives life like a party that was about to end and suddenly has the best drink of all. Jesus gives light because he sees what is inside every heart, and he loves us and wants us to be honest with him.

## 🟡 Tier 2 — Medium
### 📜 Walkthrough
#### John 2:1–2 · The Third Day and a Wedding
**Says:** "And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee; and the mother of Jesus was there" (John 2:1). Then: "And both Jesus was called, and his disciples, to the marriage." (John 2:2) *Called* here means invited. The mother of Jesus is present first; Jesus and the handful of disciples from John 1 come as guests. John never tells us her name in his Gospel; she is always 'the mother of Jesus'.

**Means:** 'The third day' most naturally counts from the last day John mentioned, when Jesus set out for Galilee and called Philip (John 1:43). John has been marking days since the Baptist's testimony (John 1:29, 35, 43), and some readers see a deliberate week of new beginnings to match the Gospel's first words, "In the beginning was the Word" (John 1:1). That is a reading, not something John states, and it should be held lightly. For a Christian reader, 'the third day' also carries the ring of resurrection, and the chapter itself will speak of raising a temple 'in three days' (John 2:19).

The setting matters more than the count. In the prophets, the LORD pictures himself as Israel's bridegroom, "as the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride, so shall thy God rejoice over thee" (Isaiah 62:5), and the age to come is pictured as a feast "of wines on the lees well refined" (Isaiah 25:6). In this Gospel, John the Baptist will call Jesus the bridegroom (John 3:29). So the first sign happens at a wedding, where Jesus is a guest but, in John's larger design, the true Bridegroom is quietly present. It also matters that he came at all. The Son of God does not despise marriage or ordinary human joy; his critics would later call him "a gluttonous man, and a winebibber" (Luke 7:34) precisely because he ate and drank with people.

Mary appears here and next at the cross (John 19:25). The two scenes frame Jesus' ministry: at Cana his hour has 'not yet come', at the cross it has.

**Asks:** Do you think of Jesus as present only in the 'religious' parts of life? He came to a village wedding. Invite him into the ordinary joys of your week, and expect him to be Lord there too.

#### John 2:3–5 · They Have No Wine
**Says:** "And when they wanted wine, the mother of Jesus saith unto him, They have no wine." (John 2:3) *Wanted* means lacked. Jesus answers, "Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come" (John 2:4). She turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it" (John 2:5).

**Means:** Mary's words are a request in the form of a report. She does not tell her son what to do; she tells him what is lacking, and she clearly expects him to act.

His reply has two parts. First, 'Woman': the vocative *gunai* (G1135, John 2:4) is not rude in itself. Jesus uses it for the Samaritan woman (John 4:21), for Mary Magdalene (John 20:15), and for his mother from the cross, "Woman, behold thy son!" (John 19:26), where it cannot be cold. Yet it is not what a son would ordinarily call his mother, and it sets a respectful distance: in his messianic work Jesus acts on his Father's timing, not on family prompting. Second, 'what have I to do with thee?' is an Old Testament idiom: Jephthah to an enemy king (Judges 11:12), David to Abishai (2 Samuel 16:10), the grieving widow to Elijah (1 Kings 17:18), a demon to Jesus (Mark 1:24). Its tone ranges from hostility to mild distancing, but it always marks that the two do not share the same concern. Here it is mild: Mary's concern is the family's embarrassment; Jesus' concern is his hour.

'Mine hour is not yet come' is the first of the hour sayings that run through John. Twice more we will hear that his enemies could not seize him "because his hour was not yet come" (John 7:30), and then, as the cross approaches, "The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified" (John 12:23). The hour is his death, resurrection, and return to the Father. At the first sign he already has the cross in view (see the View A / View B panel).

Mary is not offended. She speaks her last recorded words in John, and they point away from herself: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it" (John 2:5). Readers of the Old Testament may hear Pharaoh sending the starving Egyptians to Joseph: "Go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do." (Genesis 41:55) Whether or not John intends the echo, the logic is the same: the one who has the supply is the one you obey.

**Asks:** Bring your needs to Jesus as simply as Mary did: here is what is lacking. Leave the timing and the method to him. And hear her last words in this Gospel as the word she would say to every reader: whatever he says to you, do it.

#### John 2:6–8 · Six Waterpots of Stone
**Says:** "And there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece." (John 2:6) Jesus says, "Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim." (John 2:7) Then, "Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast. And they bare it." (John 2:8) *Firkins* are large liquid measures; *bear* means carry, and *bare* is its past tense.

**Means:** John tells us what the jars were for, and that detail carries the sign. The word 'purifying', *katharismos* (G2512, John 2:6), returns in the very next chapter, where a question arises "about purifying" (John 3:25). These were the jars for the washings of Jewish custom, the washing of hands and cups and pots that the elders' tradition required (Mark 7:3–4). Stone was chosen because, in the purity tradition, it did not contract uncleanness as clay did. Jesus takes the water of ceremonial washing and turns it into the wine of the feast. The old order of purification is not mocked; it is fulfilled and surpassed. Later the letter to the Hebrews will use the same word for what Christ did on the cross, "when he had by himself purged our sins" (Hebrews 1:3).

The amount is lavish. The Greek measure behind 'firkin', *metrētēs* (G3355, John 2:6), is given by the STEPBible lexicon (Tyndale House, following Abbott-Smith) as about nine gallons, so six jars of two or three measures each held something like 108 to 162 gallons. The prophets pictured the coming age as a time when "the mountains shall drop sweet wine" (Amos 9:13). (Some find meaning in the number six; John does not comment on it.)

Notice the servants. They are *diakonoi*, household servants, and they do exactly what they are told: they fill the jars "up to the brim" (John 2:7), so that nothing could be added, and they draw and carry without seeing any change. John never describes the moment of the miracle. We are told only the result: "the water that was made wine" (John 2:9). The governor of the feast, the *architriklinos* (G755, John 2:8), was the banquet's steward, the one who arranged the tables and the food.

**Asks:** Obedience to Jesus often looks like ordinary work: carrying water, filling jars, doing the next thing. Do it fully, to the brim, even when you cannot see what he is doing with it.

#### John 2:9–10 · The Good Wine Until Now
**Says:** The governor tasted "the water that was made wine, and knew not whence it was: (but the servants which drew the water knew;)" (John 2:9), and he called the bridegroom and said, "Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now." (John 2:10) *Whence* means from where; *well drunk* means drunk freely, drunk their fill.

**Means:** John's parenthesis is the key. The man in charge does not know where the wine came from; the servants do. 'Whence' is one of John's great questions about Jesus himself. The crowds say, "we know this man whence he is" (John 7:27), and they are wrong; the Pharisees say of him, "we know not from whence he is" (John 9:29); Pilate asks him, "Whence art thou?" (John 19:9). The governor's ignorance is a small first picture of a world that tastes the gifts of Christ without knowing where they come from.

The governor's remark is a wry saying about common practice: hosts serve the best wine first, and the poorer wine once the guests' palates are dulled. The verb behind 'well drunk', *methuō* (G3184, John 2:10), can mean to become drunk, but the governor is describing a custom, not reporting on these guests, and the passage gives no approval to drunkenness, which Scripture forbids: "be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). His real point is the surprise: 'thou hast kept the good wine until now'. He speaks better than he knows. In the history of God's dealings, the best has been kept until now: God "Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son" (Hebrews 1:2).

And notice who gets the praise: the bridegroom, who had done nothing. Jesus lets it stand. The Lord of glory is content that the first sign be known only to servants and disciples.

**Asks:** Do you know where your joys come from? Those who obey him, like the servants, know. Give thanks to the true source, and be content, like Jesus, to let others have the credit.

#### John 2:11–12 · The Beginning of Signs
**Says:** "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." (John 2:11) Then "he went down to Capernaum, he, and his mother, and his brethren, and his disciples: and they continued there not many days" (John 2:12). *Brethren* means brothers.

**Means:** This verse is John's own commentary on the scene, and every phrase is weighted. 'Beginning', *archē* (G746, John 2:11), is the word of John 1:1, 'In the beginning'. This is not merely the first in a list but the sign that sets the pattern for all the rest. The KJV's 'miracles' translates *sēmeion* (G4592, John 2:11), a sign. John numbers only two, this one and the second at Cana: "This is again the second miracle that Jesus did" (John 4:54). The church has commonly counted seven signs in the ministry; that count is a reading of the Gospel, not John's own.

What the sign did: it 'manifested forth his glory'. That is John 1:14 made visible: "we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father" (John 1:14). The glory of the LORD once filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34); now it shines at a village wedding in Galilee, and it is *his* glory. The LORD says, "my glory will I not give to another" (Isaiah 42:8), yet Jesus manifests his own glory, and John will later say that Isaiah "saw his glory, and spake of him" (John 12:41). The first sign is a quiet claim to deity. There is also a contrast with Moses: the first of the plagues on Egypt turned water to blood (Exodus 7:20), a sign of judgment; the first sign of Jesus turns water to wine, a sign of joy. "For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ." (John 1:17)

What the sign produced: 'his disciples believed on him'. They had already followed him (John 1:37–51); now their faith deepens. John's phrase is believing *on* him, into his person, and that is the faith John writes to produce (John 20:31).

Verse 12 is a hinge: mother, brothers, and disciples travel together to Capernaum. His brothers are named elsewhere (Matthew 13:55), and later "neither did his brethren believe in him" (John 7:5). Christians have understood 'brethren' differently (later children of Mary and Joseph, children of Joseph by an earlier marriage, or cousins); the passage does not settle it.

**Asks:** Read the works of Jesus as signs: each one points to him. Faith grows by beholding his glory, so linger over what he has shown you of himself, and believe on him, not only on what he gives.

#### John 2:13–15 · Passover and the Scourge
**Says:** "And the Jews' passover was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem" (John 2:13). He "found in the temple those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting" (John 2:14). "And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables" (John 2:15). A *scourge* is a whip.

**Means:** This is the first Passover in John, and the feasts give the Gospel its calendar; later we will hear that another Passover "was nigh" (John 6:4), and a last one "was nigh at hand" (John 11:55). John calls it 'the Jews' passover', explaining for readers who were not Jewish. Passover recalls the lamb slain in Egypt, and John has already pointed to Jesus as "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (John 1:29).

The 'temple' in verses 14 and 15 is *hierō* (G2411, John 2:14), a form of the noun hieron: the whole sacred precinct with its courts, not the sanctuary building itself. The dealers were meeting a real need. Pilgrims needed unblemished animals, and doves were the offering the poor could afford (Leviticus 5:7). The money changers supplied the proper coin for the half shekel of the sanctuary (Exodus 30:13), commonly the silver of Tyre, prized for its purity. The law itself allowed a worshipper to turn his tithe into money and buy what he needed "unto the place which the LORD thy God shall choose" (Deuteronomy 14:25). The fault was not trade as such but trade *in the house*: the market had moved into the court where the nations were to pray (Isaiah 56:7).

Jesus makes a whip, *phragellion* (G5416, John 2:15), from cords. The Greek of verse 15 can be read so that 'them all' is spelled out by the words that follow, *both the sheep and the oxen* (the Greek pairs them with 'both... and'), which would mean the whip drove the animals; others think the traders are included. Either way, no one is said to be hurt, and no one stops him. This is Malachi's prophecy acted out: "the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple" (Malachi 3:1), and "he shall purify the sons of Levi" (Malachi 3:3).

**Asks:** Where has convenience or profit crowded God out of the places meant for him, starting with your own worship? "For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God" (1 Peter 4:17): begin at home.

#### John 2:16–17 · My Father's House
**Says:** To the dove sellers he says, "Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise." (John 2:16) *Hence* means away from here. "And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up." (John 2:17)

**Means:** 'My Father's house' is a claim. He does not say 'our Father's house' or 'God's house'. At twelve he had already said, "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" (Luke 2:49), and later his enemies will seek to kill him because he "said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God" (John 5:18). He cleanses the temple as a son in his Father's house, not as a visitor.

'House of merchandise' uses *emporion* (G1712, John 2:16), a trading place (the root of our word 'emporium'). Many commentators hear the last line of Zechariah behind it: "in that day there shall be no more the Canaanite in the house of the LORD of hosts" (Zechariah 14:21). The Hebrew word there, *kenaani* (H3669), can mean either a Canaanite or a trader; the KJV renders it 'merchant' in Proverbs 31:24. If the allusion is intended, Jesus is announcing that the promised day has begun. It is a likely allusion, not a certain one.

The disciples remembered Psalm 69, where the psalm's first line reads: "For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me." (Psalm 69:9) The Hebrew *qinah* (H7068) is ardour or jealousy, the burning devotion that will not share what belongs to God. Psalm 69 is the prayer of a righteous sufferer, and the New Testament hears Christ in it again and again: "They hated me without a cause" (John 15:25); "The reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me" (Romans 15:3); and at the cross, "in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink" (Psalm 69:21), fulfilled in John 19:28–29. So the quotation is not only about Jesus' passion in the temple court. Zeal for God's house will consume him; it will cost him his life. The whip of cords leads to the cross.

**Asks:** Whose house is the church? It is the Father's, not ours to run for our own ends. And true zeal for God's honour looks like Christ's: it spends itself for God's house rather than spending others.

#### John 2:18–20 · What Sign Shewest Thou
**Says:** "Then answered the Jews and said unto him, What sign shewest thou unto us, seeing that thou doest these things?" (John 2:18) *Shewest* means show. Jesus answers, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19). They reply, "Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days?" (John 2:20) *Rear it up* means raise it, build it.

**Means:** 'The Jews' in John often means the temple leaders and those who spoke for them in Judea, not the Jewish people as such. Jesus and all his first disciples are Jews, and Jesus himself says "salvation is of the Jews" (John 4:22). Their question is fair on its face: a man who acts with this authority in the temple should show his credentials. But they ask for a sign after seeing one; the cleansing itself was the sign of Malachi 3:1.

Jesus answers with a riddle. 'Destroy' is an imperative, but it works as a condition: destroy it, and I will raise it; if you destroy this temple, I will raise it up in three days. It is prophetic irony, not an order: they will do exactly this. His word for temple has changed from the precinct of verse 14 to *naos*, the sanctuary, the house of God's dwelling; and his word for 'raise' is the word used of raising the dead.

They take him literally, as people in John often do: Nicodemus asks how a man can "enter the second time into his mother's womb" (John 3:4). The misunderstanding lets John explain the truth. Their figure of forty-six years fits what Josephus reports: Herod began rebuilding in the eighteenth year of his reign (*Antiquities of the Jews*, book 15), about 20 or 19 BC, which dates this Passover to about AD 27 or 28, with the courts still unfinished. The irony runs deep: the building they boast of would be torn down within a lifetime, in AD 70, while the temple they destroyed would stand up on the third day. At his trial, false witnesses would twist this saying into a threat against the building, "I will destroy this temple that is made with hands" (Mark 14:58), and the mockers would throw it at him on the cross (Mark 15:29). John preserves what he actually said.

**Asks:** Do we, too, demand that God prove himself on our terms before we trust him? He has given the sign that matters, the death and resurrection of his Son. Stop asking for a different one.

#### John 2:21–22 · The Temple of His Body
**Says:** "But he spake of the temple of his body." (John 2:21) "When therefore he was risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this unto them; and they believed the scripture, and the word which Jesus had said." (John 2:22)

**Means:** Here the narrator steps in and tells us what the disciples themselves did not understand at the time. John writes from the far side of the resurrection, and he tells us so; the same thing happens at the entry into Jerusalem: "These things understood not his disciples at the first: but when Jesus was glorified, then remembered they" (John 12:16). Jesus had promised that the Spirit would "bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you" (John 14:26). The remembering in verse 22 is that promise at work.

The temple was where God put his name and his presence among his people: "let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them" (Exodus 25:8). Even Solomon knew the building could not contain God (1 Kings 8:27). Now John says that Jesus' own body is the temple. The Word "dwelt among us" (John 1:14), and in him "dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily" (Colossians 2:9). The place where God meets men is no longer a building in Jerusalem but a Person, crucified and raised. From him the temple extends to his people, "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God" (1 Corinthians 3:16), and at the end the city needs no temple, "for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it" (Revelation 21:22).

'They believed the scripture': John does not say which. It may be Psalm 69, or the Scriptures that foretold his rising "according to the scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:4), such as Psalm 16:10. And John sets 'the scripture' and 'the word which Jesus had said' side by side: Jesus' words stand with the Old Testament as the word of God.

**Asks:** Faith grows by remembering: Scripture recalled and the words of Jesus believed, read in the light of his resurrection. What have you read in Scripture that you did not understand then, and that makes sense now that you know him better?

#### John 2:23–25 · He Knew What Was in Man
**Says:** "Now when he was in Jerusalem at the passover, in the feast day, many believed in his name, when they saw the miracles which he did." (John 2:23) "But Jesus did not commit himself unto them, because he knew all men" (John 2:24), "And needed not that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man." (John 2:25) *Commit himself* means entrust himself; *testify of* means bear witness about.

**Means:** John makes a play on one verb. Many 'believed' (*pisteuō*) in his name, but Jesus did not 'commit' himself to them, and the word for 'commit' is the same verb: they trusted in him, but he did not trust himself to them. The phrase 'believed in his name' can describe saving faith; the Prologue promised power to become the sons of God "even to them that believe on his name" (John 1:12). So the same outward words can describe a faith that is real and a faith that is not yet. The difference lies in the heart, and only he can see it.

Faith that begins with the signs is not worthless. Jesus himself says, "believe me for the very works' sake" (John 14:11). But faith that rests on the signs alone does not last. Later a crowd follows him for the loaves (John 6:26), and "many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him" (John 6:66). In John 8, those who 'believed on him' (John 8:30–31) end the chapter taking up stones (John 8:59).

Jesus' knowledge of hearts runs through this Gospel. He knows Nathanael before they meet (John 1:47–48), the Samaritan woman's history (John 4:18), and Judas from the beginning (John 6:64). Peter will finally say, "Lord, thou knowest all things" (John 21:17). In the Old Testament this is God's own knowledge: "thou, even thou only, knowest the hearts of all the children of men" (1 Kings 8:39). Jesus has it without being told. 'Testify', *martureō*, is John's witness word: people need witness about Jesus, but Jesus needs no witness about people.

These verses also lead straight into chapter 3. John has just said that Jesus 'knew what was in man', and the next sentence begins, "There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus" (John 3:1). Nicodemus comes impressed by the signs, and Jesus will show what is in him.

**Asks:** Examine your own faith, not to torment yourself but to be honest: is it resting on him, or on what he gives? He already knows what is in you, so come to him openly; there is nothing to hide from one who sees it all and still invites you.

### 🚫 Common Errors Quick-Reference
| Error | Why it is wrong | The correction, with verse |
|---|---|---|
| Cana means that if I obey, Jesus will make my life prosperous and my celebrations never run short. | The wine is a sign of his glory and of the new covenant, not a guarantee of comfort. The same Jesus was given vinegar on the cross, and his hour was his death. Abundant life means fullness of life in Christ. | The life Christ gives is himself (John 10:10); his hour was the cross (John 12:23). |
| The temple cleansing gives me licence to expose and shame other Christians whose worship I dislike. | Jesus is the Lord of the house; we are not. His zeal consumed himself, not others. Being light begins with my own heart and is carried in love. | We reprove darkness while speaking the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), and our own body is the first temple to be cleansed (1 Corinthians 6:19). |
| Jesus was rude to his mother; or, Mary is the one who obtains grace from Jesus for us. | 'Woman' is a respectful address Jesus also uses at the cross, but it marks that his hour is set by the Father. Mary's own words direct all attention to her Son. | "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it" (John 2:5); his care for her at the cross (John 19:26–27). |
| Faith that is excited by miracles is saving faith, so what people need most is more wonders. | John shows many believing because of the signs, while Jesus does not entrust himself to them. Signs point to him; faith must rest on him. | "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed" (John 20:29) |

### 🧨 Cultural Landmines and Misconceptions
**Was it real wine?** Some Christians hold that Jesus made unfermented grape juice. The word is the ordinary word for wine, and the governor's remark assumes wine that could dull the palate. Scripture treats wine as a gift (Psalm 104:15) and condemns drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18). Do not let this question swallow the sign; see Tough Question 1 in the Leader's Guide.

**The Jews in John.** Modern readers can hear 'the Jews' in John 2:18–20 as a blanket charge against the Jewish people, and that reading has fed terrible sins in church history. In John the phrase often means the Judean religious leaders who opposed Jesus. Jesus, his mother, and all his first disciples were Jews, and it is Jesus who says "salvation is of the Jews" (John 4:22). Teach this chapter without a trace of contempt.

**The money changers were not simply crooks.** In the later cleansing Jesus calls the temple 'a den of thieves' (Mark 11:17), but in John the charge is different: making the Father's house a 'house of merchandise' (John 2:16). The fault in John 2 is not first of all cheating; it is the market in the house, business crowding out prayer. That is a sharper word for churches today, because it can apply even when everyone is honest.

**Stone jars and purity.** The jars were not drinking-water jars; John says they served 'the purifying of the Jews', and stone vessels from this period are common finds in Judea and Galilee.

## 🔴 Tier 3 — Expert
### 🏗️ Theological Framework
John 2 sits at the meeting point of Christology and the doctrine of worship, and it is best read through the Reformed conviction that Scripture interprets Scripture and that the whole Old Testament economy was a shadow whose body is Christ: "Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ." (Colossians 2:17)

*Christology.* Three features quietly assert deity: Jesus manifests *his* glory (John 2:11; Isaiah 42:8), calls the temple 'my Father's house' (John 2:16; John 5:18), and knows what is in man without being told (John 2:25; 1 Kings 8:39). The chapter also shows the Son's submission to the Father's hour and his own power over his life (John 2:19; John 10:17–18).

*Covenant and fulfilment.* The chapter is a study in replacement by fulfilment. The water of purification becomes wine; the temple of stone gives way to the temple of his body. The Westminster Confession (chapter 19) teaches that the ceremonial laws, given to Israel as a church under age, prefigured Christ and are now abrogated under the new testament; John 2 is one of the places where the reader watches that happen. The wine anticipates the cup of the new covenant, "This cup is the new testament in my blood" (Luke 22:20), and the feast of the kingdom, when Jesus will drink the fruit of the vine "new in the kingdom of God" (Mark 14:25).

*Temple theology.* Scripture traces one line: God dwelling with his people in the tabernacle (Exodus 25:8), the temple Solomon knew could not contain him (1 Kings 8:27), the prophets' visions of a greater house (Haggai 2:9; Ezekiel 47:1), the Word who tabernacled among us (John 1:14), the body destroyed and raised (John 2:19–21), the church built into a holy temple in him (Ephesians 2:21–22), and the city whose temple is the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb (Revelation 21:22). John 2 is the hinge of that line.

*Worship and faith.* Because God is present in Christ, acceptable worship is defined by Christ and his word, not by human commerce or invention (the regulative principle; John 4:21–24 completes what John 2 begins). And true understanding comes after the resurrection, through remembered Scripture and the Spirit's teaching (John 2:22; John 14:26): faith is a gift worked through the word, resting on a person.

### 📚 Scholarly Insights
- **Augustine**, *Tractates on the Gospel of John* (the tractates on John 2): reads the water made wine as the Old Testament whose meaning becomes sweet and plain once Christ is understood in it, and treats the six jars as six ages of the world (verify the detail of the six ages). Whatever one thinks of the allegory, his central instinct, that the sign concerns Christ as the meaning of the Scriptures, fits John 2:22.
- **John Calvin**, *Commentary on the Gospel According to John*: reads 'Woman, what have I to do with thee?' as a deliberate check, so that no one would later make Mary a partner in Christ's divine work (verify), and treats the cleansing in John as distinct from the one the other Gospels place in the last week (verify). He presses the application to worship corrupted by gain.
- **J. C. Ryle**, *Expository Thoughts on the Gospels* (John): draws practical lessons: Christ's presence at a wedding honours marriage and lawful joy; Christ's words to his mother guard against giving Mary the honour due to him; and the cleansing warns against irreverence and profit-seeking in the things of God (verify the particular points).
- **D. A. Carson**, *The Gospel According to John* (Pillar New Testament Commentary, 1991): argues that the chronological markers in John 2:12–23 and the differences from the Synoptic accounts favour two cleansings, and reads John 2:23–25 as describing a faith that is spurious or at least inadequate (verify).
- **Raymond E. Brown**, *The Gospel According to John* (Anchor Bible, 1966): emphasises the theme of replacement in John 2–4 (wine for purification water, the body for the temple, new birth, worship in spirit and truth) and holds that there was one cleansing, which John has placed early for theological reasons (verify).

### ⚔️ Debate Corner
**The question:** Did Jesus cleanse the temple twice, once near the start of his ministry (John 2:13–22) and once in the last week (Mark 11:15–17), or is there one event that John and the Synoptic Gospels place differently?

**Position 1 · One cleansing, placed early by John for theological reasons.** Many modern scholars (Brown among them) hold that the event happened in the last week, as the Synoptics narrate, and that John moved it to the front as a programmatic scene: the temple is replaced by Jesus, and the conflict that ends in the cross is announced at once. Ancient historians did arrange material topically, and some evangelical scholars hold a version of this view without conceding error, arguing that John makes no chronological claim here.

**Position 2 · One cleansing, placed correctly by John.** A few argue that John's early date is the historical one, and that Mark, who narrates only one visit to Jerusalem, placed the event in the only Jerusalem week his outline had. Its weakness is that the cleansing fits well as the trigger of the final conflict (Mark 11:18).

**Position 3 · Two cleansings.** Calvin and many Reformed and evangelical commentators (Carson and Leon Morris among them, verify) hold that Jesus did this twice. They point out that John's markers are explicitly chronological ('After this', 'the Jews' passover was at hand', 'forty and six years', John 2:12–13, 20); that the details differ (the whip, sheep and oxen, 'house of merchandise' and Psalm 69 in John, against 'den of thieves' with Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11 in the Synoptics); and that the Synoptics' trial scene reports a saying about destroying and building the temple in three days (Mark 14:58) which only John narrates, suggesting it was spoken earlier. A repeated prophetic act at the beginning and end of a ministry is not strange; it would be a fitting frame.

**Most consistent with Reformed hermeneutics.** The Reformed approach reads each text in its own terms and lets Scripture interpret Scripture, confident that the Gospels are true in everything they affirm. That confidence does not by itself decide between Positions 1 and 3, since a topical arrangement is not an error if the author makes no chronological claim. The question is what John claims. Here John goes out of his way to give time markers, and the two accounts differ at almost every point of detail and interpretation. Reading John's words as he wrote them, the two-cleansing view is the most natural and the least strained, and it is the view this study holds. It should be held humbly: faithful scholars differ, and nothing in the chapter's teaching depends on the answer.

**Pastoral Warning:** A church can spend an evening on the chronology and go home unchanged. The chapter's question is not 'how many times?' but 'what would the Lord find if he came suddenly to his temple today, in my heart and in our church?' Be careful, too, with new believers: do not introduce the debate as though the Gospels were at war, and do not wave away honest questions with scorn. Teach the harmony calmly, and then turn to the Lord of the house.

### 🔤 Original Language Deep Dive
Every definition below comes from one source: the brief Greek and Hebrew lexicon published by STEPBible.org (Tyndale House, Cambridge), whose Greek entries are drawn largely from G. Abbott-Smith, *A Manual Greek Lexicon of the New Testament*. It is called 'the STEPBible lexicon' below.

**The play on 'believe' in John 2:23–24.** Verse 23 says many believed: *episteusan* (G4100, John 2:23, V-AAI-3P), an aorist. Verse 24 says Jesus did not commit himself to them: *episteuen* (G4100, John 2:24, V-IAI-3S), the imperfect of the same verb with a reflexive object, 'he was not entrusting himself'. The KJV's 'commit' is accurate but hides the echo. The STEPBible lexicon notes the range of constructions this verb takes in the New Testament; John's favourite for saving faith is the verb with *eis*, believing 'into' or 'on' a person, the very construction of John 2:11, *episteusan* (G4100, John 2:11, V-AAI-3P) with *eis auton*. In the KJV of John, words beginning 'believ' occur 101 times, and in John 2 they occur 3 times (John 2:11, 22, 23); the Greek verb appears a fourth time behind 'commit' in verse 24. John is not interested in belief as a feeling, but in whether a person entrusts himself to Jesus, and whether Jesus can entrust himself to that person.

**Two words for temple.** In verses 14–15 the word is the neuter noun hieron, here *hierou* (G2411, John 2:15, N-GSN), not the adjective *hieros* (G2413, 2 Timothy 3:15), 'sacred', from which it is formed. The STEPBible lexicon defines hieron as the whole sacred precinct, 'as distinct from' the sanctuary proper. In verses 19–21 the word is *naos* (G3485, John 2:20), which the same lexicon defines as the sanctuary, the temple building proper, and it lists John 2:19–20 under that sense. Jesus cleanses the courts, but when he speaks of his body he chooses the word for the dwelling place of God. This is a real distinction in the STEPBible lexicon, though it should not be pressed into a rule for every New Testament use.

**'Destroy' and 'raise'.** *Lusate* (G3089, John 2:19, V-AAM-2P) is an aorist imperative of a verb whose basic sense is to loose; the STEPBible lexicon lists 'loosen, dissolve, break up, destroy' and cites John 2:19 under that sense. An imperative followed by 'and' with a future verb often carries the force of a condition: 'destroy..., and I will raise' means 'if you destroy..., I will raise'. The future *egerō* (G1453, John 2:19, V-FAI-1S) is the verb the New Testament uses for raising the dead; the STEPBible lexicon lists 'to raise from the dead' among its chief senses and cites John 2:22 for the passive. In verse 22 the same verb is passive: *ēgerthē* (G1453, John 2:22, V-API-3S), 'he was raised'. The active in verse 19 makes Jesus the one who raises; the passive in verse 22 points to God as the one who raised him. Scripture affirms both (John 10:18; Galatians 1:1).

**'Was in building'.** *Oikodomēthē* (G3618, John 2:20, V-API-3S) is an aorist passive; the KJV takes it as summing up forty-six years of work to date. Some take it of the sanctuary proper, finished forty-six years earlier; either way the date falls in the late twenties AD.

**'Hath eaten me up'.** The Textus Receptus behind the KJV reads *katephagen* (G2719, John 2:17, V-2AAI-3S), an aorist, 'hath eaten me up', matching the psalm. Many modern editions of the Greek text read a future here ('shall eat me up'), which would point more plainly forward to the cross. The verb in either reading is a strong compound meaning to devour; the STEPBible lexicon lists John 2:17 among its uses with a personal object. The Hebrew behind Psalm 69:9, *qinah* (H7068), is defined in the STEPBible lexicon as ardour, zeal, and jealousy, including zeal 'for the house of God'.

**Sign.** *Sēmeion* (G4592, John 2:18) in the Greek Old Testament chiefly renders the Hebrew for a sign, the word used of the signs in Egypt (Exodus 4:30). John's choice of 'sign' invites the reader to look through the work to the worker.

### 🚷 Preaching Mistakes to Avoid
- **Information without life:** a lecture on first-century weddings, firkins, and Herod's building programme that never brings the hearer to the Bridegroom, the true temple, and the call to believe on him.
- **Heat without light:** preaching the cleansing as licence for anger at 'worldly churches', with no cross. Jesus' zeal consumed himself, not his hearers; a sermon that leaves people angry at others and unexamined themselves has missed the text.
- **Moralism at Cana:** 'Do whatever he says, and your water will turn to wine.' Obedience is the right response to Jesus, but it is not a technique for getting results; the sign is about his glory.
- **Mary made too much of, or too little:** making her the channel of grace, or speaking of her with disrespect. She points away from herself to her Son (John 2:5).
- **Allegory without restraint:** hidden meanings for the six jars or the governor. Say what John says, and mark any suggestion as a suggestion.

## 🟣 Tier 4 — Christocentric, Humility, Life & Light
### 👑 Every Answer in Jesus
John 2 leaves no room for self-glory. Every character in it is exposed as needing Jesus: the bridegroom who could not supply his own feast, the mother whose request must yield to the Father's hour, the governor who praised the wrong man, the traders who turned God's house to profit, the leaders who demanded a sign and missed the one in front of them, the disciples who understood only after the resurrection, and the many whose faith Jesus would not trust. No one in the chapter supplies the wine, cleanses the house, or raises the temple except Jesus.

And every good thing the chapter holds is found in him. The joy of the feast is his gift. The purity the jars could only picture is his work. The presence of God the temple housed dwells bodily in him. The sign the leaders demanded is his own resurrection. The knowledge that searches the heart is his. This is what Paul means when he says of Christ, "In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." (Colossians 2:3) The chapter humbles us by showing that we contribute nothing but empty jars and obedience, and it makes Christ glorious by showing that he fills them.

### 🙇 Humility Practices
- Before you lead this study, pray the publican's prayer honestly for one minute, "God be merciful to me a sinner" (Luke 18:13), and ask the Lord to cleanse your own motives for teaching.
- Take one task this week that no one will see or thank you for (setting up chairs, washing cups, clearing up after the group) and do it as to the Lord, who "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:7).
- When someone in your group gives a better answer than yours, say so aloud and thank them, practising the humility God rewards, for he "giveth grace unto the humble" (James 4:6).

### 🌱 Life Practices
- **Inward:** Each morning this week, before looking at your phone, read one verse of John 2 and thank Jesus for one specific gift of his that you did not make, acknowledging that "without me ye can do nothing" (John 15:5).
- **Outward:** Identify one couple in your church or neighbourhood whose marriage seems to have run dry (__________), and do one concrete kindness for them this week (a meal, an offer to watch their children, a note), praying for the Lord who gives good wine to renew them (John 2:10).
- **Outward:** Invite one person who has drifted from church (__________) to come to the group or to Sunday worship with you, telling them that God's house is a place to meet him, not a market (John 2:16).

### 💡 Light Practices
- **Inward:** Write down every reason you went to church last Sunday, the honourable ones and the others, and bring the list to the Lord who "knew what was in man" (John 2:25), confessing what needs confessing (1 John 1:9).
- **Outward:** If there is a practice in your ministry that has quietly turned toward profit or self-promotion, raise it with one fellow leader this week, gently and privately, as the Lord's zeal for his Father's house requires (John 2:16; Ephesians 4:15).
- **Outward:** Share John 2:19–22 with one person who thinks Christianity is about being religious (__________), showing them that God's presence is found in the risen Jesus, not in a building (John 2:21).

## 📚 Doctrine
### Theology Proper · The Father Is Jealous for His House and Defines His Worship
**Proposition:** God the Father claims the place of his worship as his own house, and he, not the worshipper, decides what is fitting there. His zeal for his honour is holy jealousy: the love that refuses to share with rivals what belongs to him alone.

**Textual Anchor:** Jesus calls the temple "my Father's house" (John 2:16) and forbids making it "an house of merchandise" (John 2:16); the disciples recognise in his act the zeal of Psalm 69: "The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up" (John 2:17).

**Cross-References:** "Is this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, even I have seen it, saith the LORD." (Jeremiah 7:11); "for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people" (Isaiah 56:7); "For our God is a consuming fire." (Hebrews 12:29)

**Errors Refuted:** (1) *Sincerity is all that matters in worship.* Its holders would say: 'God looks on the heart, so the form of worship is ours to choose, as long as we mean it.' John 2 answers that God looks on the heart *and* judges the practice: the traders may have been sincere and useful, and Jesus still drove the market out, because the house is the Father's. (2) *Jealousy is beneath God.* God's jealousy is not insecurity but the loving claim of a husband on his bride and of the Creator on his worship, and the Son shares it to the point of death (Psalm 69:9).

**Pastoral Fruit:** Reverence: coming into worship aware whose house it is. Self-examination: asking honestly whether any practice in our church serves our convenience or profit more than prayer. And love for God's house, "LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house" (Psalm 26:8), without idolising a building.

### Christology · The Glory of the Son Manifested in the Sign
**Proposition:** In the sign at Cana, Jesus revealed his own glory, the glory of the only begotten of the Father, showing himself Lord over creation and the giver of the joy of the promised age; the glory is his by right, as God.

**Textual Anchor:** John says Jesus "manifested forth his glory" (John 2:11), and the sign is a real act over creation: the governor tasted "the water that was made wine" (John 2:9).

**Cross-References:** "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth." (John 1:14); "I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images." (Isaiah 42:8); "These things said Esaias, when he saw his glory, and spake of him." (John 12:41)

**Errors Refuted:** (1) *Jesus is a glorious creature, not God.* Arius in the early church, and the Watchtower Society today, hold that the Son is the first and highest of God's creatures, who reflects God's glory. But the LORD gives his glory to no other (Isaiah 42:8), while John says Jesus manifests *his* glory and identifies the glory Isaiah saw in the temple as the glory of Jesus (John 12:41). (2) *The story is a symbolic legend.* Many modern critics read Cana as a parable told in narrative form, with no event behind it. John presents it as a dated, located act with witnesses (the servants knew, the disciples believed), and he rests his whole purpose on real signs done "in the presence of his disciples" (John 20:30).

**Pastoral Fruit:** Worship: the Jesus we pray to is the Lord of glory, not a helpful teacher. Confidence: he is Lord over the ordinary stuff of life, water and jars and weddings. And humility: the glory is his, so we stop seeking our own.

### Christology · The Body of Jesus, the True Temple
**Proposition:** Jesus' own body, crucified and raised, is the true temple: the place where God dwells with men and where sinners meet God. His bodily resurrection on the third day is the sign that proves his authority over the house of God.

**Textual Anchor:** Jesus says, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19), and John explains, "But he spake of the temple of his body." (John 2:21) The temple destroyed is the body that dies, and the temple raised is the same body.

**Cross-References:** "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily." (Colossians 2:9); "But I say unto you, That in this place is one greater than the temple." (Matthew 12:6); "And I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it." (Revelation 21:22)

**Errors Refuted:** (1) *God is met more truly in sacred places.* Some traditions hold that particular buildings, shrines, or sites make worship more acceptable or grace more available. John 2 moves the meeting place of God and man from a building to a person, and John 4:21–24 completes the move. (2) *A future temple as a means of access.* Some Christians expect a rebuilt temple with renewed sacrifices in a future age; most who hold this say the sacrifices would be memorials, not atonements. Whatever one concludes about Ezekiel 40–48, access to God is now through the risen Christ alone, "By a new and living way... through the veil, that is to say, his flesh" (Hebrews 10:20). (3) *A spiritual rather than bodily resurrection.* Some say only Jesus' cause lived on. But the temple raised is the temple destroyed, his body (John 2:21).

**Pastoral Fruit:** Access: a believer can meet God anywhere, because God is met in Christ. Assurance: the resurrection proves that his claims are true. Hope: the body destroyed and raised is the pattern of our own resurrection (Romans 8:11).

### Christology · The Son Who Knows What Is in Man
**Proposition:** Jesus knows the hearts of all people in his own person, without being told, with the knowledge Scripture ascribes to God alone, and he acts on that knowledge.

**Textual Anchor:** "he knew all men" (John 2:24), and he "needed not that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man" (John 2:25).

**Cross-References:** "for thou, even thou only, knowest the hearts of all the children of men" (1 Kings 8:39); "Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do." (Hebrews 4:13); "Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee" (John 21:17)

**Errors Refuted:** (1) *The Son gave up divine knowledge in the incarnation.* Some kenotic theologies hold that the Son laid aside omniscience (or its use) to live a truly human life, pointing to Luke 2:52 and Mark 13:32. Those texts are real: in his human nature Jesus grew in wisdom and did not know the day of his return. But John 2:24–25 shows him knowing hearts as only God does. The Chalcedonian confession, held by the Reformed churches, keeps both: one person in two natures, each keeping its own properties. (2) *Jesus was merely perceptive.* John sets this knowledge in the language of God's own (1 Kings 8:39), and Peter confesses it as knowing all things (John 21:17).

**Pastoral Fruit:** Comfort: we are fully known by the one who died for us, and nothing in us will surprise him. Honesty: pretending before him is pointless, so confession becomes easy. And caution: we cannot see hearts as he does, so we leave final judgments of others to him (1 Corinthians 4:5).

### Anthropology & Sin · Hearts That Trade on God and Trust in Signs
**Proposition:** Fallen human beings turn even the worship and the gifts of God into means to their own ends: they make the Father's house a market, and they follow Jesus for what he shows, while the heart remains unsurrendered. Religious privilege does not cure this.

**Textual Anchor:** In the very house of God, Jesus finds "an house of merchandise" (John 2:16); in the holy city at the holy feast, many believe "when they saw the miracles which he did" (John 2:23), yet "Jesus did not commit himself unto them" (John 2:24).

**Cross-References:** "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" (Jeremiah 17:9); "Ye seek me, not because ye saw the miracles, but because ye did eat of the loaves, and were filled." (John 6:26); "For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom:" (1 Corinthians 1:22)

**Errors Refuted:** (1) *People are basically good and need a better environment.* Its holders say sin is mostly the product of bad surroundings. John 2 shows sin thriving in the best religious environment the world had, the temple at Passover. (2) *Any profession of faith proves new birth.* Some evangelistic practice treats every raised hand as conversion. John 2:23–24 shows people 'believing in his name' in a way Jesus does not trust. This is not a tool to torment weak believers but a call to rest on Christ and continue in his word (John 8:31).

**Pastoral Fruit:** Humility: I am capable of the same trade and the same shallow faith. Watchfulness over motives in ministry. And an evangelism that aims at faith in Christ himself, not at excitement or numbers.

### Soteriology & Grace · The Good Wine of the New Covenant
**Proposition:** What the ceremonial washings could only picture, Christ supplies: cleansing and joy given freely by his grace, better than all that came before, received by believing on him.

**Textual Anchor:** The water came from jars kept "after the manner of the purifying of the Jews" (John 2:6), and it became wine of which the governor said, "thou hast kept the good wine until now" (John 2:10); the result was that "his disciples believed on him" (John 2:11).

**Cross-References:** "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price." (Isaiah 55:1); "For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect." (Hebrews 10:1); "And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace." (John 1:16)

**Errors Refuted:** (1) *Grace is conveyed by the rite itself.* Some traditions teach that sacraments confer grace by the act performed, where no obstacle is placed. The Reformed churches hold that sacraments are signs and seals made effective by the Spirit through faith; at Cana the water became wine by Christ's word, not by the vessel. (2) *We are made clean by adding duties.* The jars were full to the brim and still could not supply the feast. (3) *Free grace means licence.* The servants who received the gift were the ones who obeyed.

**Pastoral Fruit:** Joy: the Christian life is a wedding feast, not a washing routine. Rest: we stop trying to purify ourselves by performance. Generosity: those who have been given wine without price give freely.

### Christian Walk · Whatsoever He Saith unto You, Do It
**Proposition:** The disciple's walk is ready and complete obedience to the word of Christ, trusting him before seeing the outcome, doing ordinary tasks at his command, and letting him have the glory.

**Textual Anchor:** Mary's charge, "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it" (John 2:5), and the servants' response: "And they filled them up to the brim." (John 2:7)

**Cross-References:** "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word" (Luke 1:38); "If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed" (John 8:31); "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." (1 Corinthians 10:31)

**Errors Refuted:** (1) *Obedience is a technique for getting results.* Prosperity teaching says: obey, give, and declare, and God is bound to bless you materially. The servants obeyed without being promised anything, and the sign was for Christ's glory, not their gain. (2) *Faith without obedience.* Some teach that believing requires no following. John's disciples believe and continue; Jesus defines disciples as those who continue in his word (John 8:31).

**Pastoral Fruit:** Promptness: doing the next thing he says without waiting to understand it. Faithfulness in small, unseen tasks. And a quiet heart that does not need to know the result before it obeys.

### Assumed Here
- **Pneumatology:** The Spirit is not named in John 2, but the disciples' remembering after the resurrection (John 2:22) is the work Jesus later assigns to the Holy Ghost (John 14:26), and believers become God's temple because the Spirit dwells in them (1 Corinthians 3:16).
- **Ecclesiology:** The chapter assumes a community gathered around Jesus, 'his disciples' (John 2:11), and anticipates a people built into a temple in him, taught plainly in Ephesians 2:21–22 and 1 Peter 2:5.
- **Eschatology:** The wedding and the good wine anticipate the feast of the age to come (Isaiah 25:6; Revelation 19:9), and the raised temple anticipates the city whose temple is the Lamb (Revelation 21:22); the chapter points there but does not teach the last things directly.

## ⚖️ The Council's Hard Questions
### ❓ Question 1 · Did Jesus Rebuke His Mother, and What Is His Hour
**Moderator:** John 2:4 troubles many readers. 'Woman, what have I to do with thee?' sounds harsh, and 'mine hour' is not explained. Is this a rebuke, and what hour does he mean?

**Philologist:** Start with the words. The vocative 'woman' is a courteous address in Greek; Jesus uses it for his mother again from the cross (John 19:26), in a moment of tender care. The question is a Hebrew idiom found in Judges 11:12, 2 Samuel 16:10, and 1 Kings 17:18. It marks a difference of concern between two people, and its tone depends on context. Here, I would call it a gentle distancing, not a scolding.

**Historian:** And it is striking that a son would use 'woman' to his mother at all. It is not how sons normally spoke. That suggests Jesus is stepping outside the family relationship: in this matter, he is not acting as Mary's son but as the one sent by the Father.

**Church Historian:** Roman Catholic teaching sees at Cana Mary's intercession moving her Son to act, and draws from it her role as intercessor for the church; it notices, rightly, that her request was followed by the sign. Many Protestant commentators, Calvin among them (verify), read the words as a deliberate check against giving Mary any share in Christ's authority.

**Theologian:** But notice the order. Mary makes her request, Jesus declares that his action answers to his hour, and Mary directs the servants to *him*. She claims no power of her own. Her last words in this Gospel are 'Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.' And 'mine hour' in John always points to the cross (John 7:30; John 8:20; John 12:23; John 13:1; John 17:1). At the first sign, he is thinking of the hour when his glory will be fully shown.

**Pastor:** For our group this is less a controversy than a pattern for prayer: bring the need, accept his timing, and trust him anyway.

**Resolution:** Jesus does not dishonour his mother. He addresses her with respect, marks that his work answers to the Father's hour and not to family request, and then acts. Mary models faith by pointing away from herself to her Son (John 2:5). 'Mine hour' is best read with the rest of John as the hour of his death and glory (John 12:23), already in view at the first sign; the sign itself is a foretaste of that glory.

### ❓ Question 2 · Who Raised Jesus from the Dead
**Moderator:** In John 2:19 Jesus says 'I will raise it up.' But elsewhere Scripture says God raised him. Did Jesus raise himself, or was he raised?

**Philologist:** The grammar shows both. John 2:19 uses the active future, 'I will raise'. John 2:22 uses the passive, 'he was raised', which Greek often uses when God is the unstated actor. John saw no contradiction in placing them three verses apart.

**Theologian:** Scripture attributes the resurrection to each person of the Trinity. The Father: "God the Father, who raised him from the dead" (Galatians 1:1). The Son: "I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again" (John 10:18). The Spirit: "the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead" (Romans 8:11). This is the old rule that the outward works of the Trinity are undivided. The one God raised Jesus, and each person shares in the act in his own way.

**Literary Scholar:** And John makes a dramatic point with it. The leaders ask for a sign of authority. Jesus answers that his authority will be proven by an act only God can do, and that he himself will do it. The man who has just cleansed the Father's house claims to be able to rebuild the temple of his own body.

**Teacher:** For a new believer I would put it simply: God raised Jesus, and Jesus is God. The Father, the Son, and the Spirit always work together.

**Resolution:** Both statements are true, and they belong together. The Father raised the Son (Galatians 1:1), the Son took up his own life by his own power (John 10:18), and the Spirit gave life to his mortal body (Romans 8:11). John 2:19 is a claim to divine authority, and John 2:22 shows its fulfilment.

### ❓ Question 3 · Why Would Jesus Not Entrust Himself to Believers
**Moderator:** John 2:23 says many 'believed in his name', the language of John 1:12. Yet Jesus did not commit himself to them. Were they saved or not, and what should we do with this?

**Literary Scholar:** John is making a deliberate play with one verb. They 'believed', and he did not 'believe himself' to them. That is a narrator's warning placed right before Nicodemus, who comes because of the signs (John 3:2). John is teaching us to ask what kind of faith we are looking at.

**Historian:** It is Passover in Jerusalem, crowded with pilgrims and full of national hope. Signs from a prophet would stir hopes of liberation, as when a crowd later wanted to make him king (John 6:15). Jesus would not hand himself over to hopes like that.

**Theologian:** Scripture distinguishes an early response from faith that rests on Christ. The sower parable speaks of those who "for a while believe" (Luke 8:13) and fall away. The Reformed tradition calls this 'temporary faith', and holds that saving faith is the Spirit's gift, rooted in Christ and shown by continuing in his word (John 8:31). We cannot always tell the difference from outside; Jesus could.

**Pastor:** And that must be handled gently. Some in our group will hear this and fear their faith is fake. The answer is not to stare at the quality of our faith but to look again at Christ. Faith that looks to him, however weak, is the faith he receives: "him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out" (John 6:37).

**Teacher:** For the lesson, I want participants to see the difference between the disciples in verse 11, who saw his glory and believed on him, and the crowd in verse 23, who saw his signs. That contrast can be seen by anyone at Level 1.

**Resolution:** John does not tell us the final state of every person in the Passover crowd. He tells us that their faith was not yet the kind Jesus would entrust himself to, because it rested on the signs rather than on him, and he knew their hearts (John 2:24–25). The remedy is not introspection but looking to Christ: the faith that saves is faith that comes to him and continues in his word (John 6:37; John 8:31).

### 🔦 The Life & Light Audit
**Pastor:** If a hearer obeyed this lesson exactly, the place where their wine had run out would be named to Jesus in prayer, and one dry person nearby, a widow, a lonely neighbour, a couple whose marriage has gone flat, would receive a visit, a meal, or a word about where the good wine comes from. The dark place lit would be the hearer's own motives in worship.

**Theologian:** The practices keep source discipline. None asks the hearer to produce joy or purity; each brings an empty jar to Christ and carries what he gives, like the servants who obeyed and carried but did not make the wine (John 2:7–9). The Light practices begin with the heart and are shaped by the Love Guard.

**Teacher:** A Level 1 participant can do the Inward Life practice tonight and the Humility Practice of hidden service this week. The Outward practices name the kind of person to reach and leave a blank for the name, so a newcomer knows exactly what to do.

**Fix:** The Audit asked for two changes, and both are in the unit. The Outward Life practices name the kind of person to reach (a widow, a lonely neighbour, a discouraged friend; a person outside the church) instead of a general 'someone'; and the Gather naming round tells members to read the second row of the Light Planner, never the private first row, so that the light is carried in love and no one is exposed.

## 🗝️ Leader's Guide
### ⏱️ Session Plan
| Segment | Minutes | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Open: prayer and warm-up | 5 | Pray Psalm 119:18 together; two or three share answers to the warm-up. |
| Setting the Scene and Read & Mark | 12 | The leader reads Setting the Scene aloud (2 minutes); two readers read John 2 aloud, one for each scene, while everyone marks their text. |
| Observe, Mind the Language, Word Study | 8 | Work through Q1–Q6 quickly as a group; fill in the Mind the Language blanks together; point to one Word Study row, the play on 'believe' and 'commit'. |
| Search the Scriptures and Interpret | 12 | Read two of the cross-references aloud; discuss Q8–Q10; take the View A / View B panel and Q11. |
| Group questions 1 to 3 | 20 | Gather questions 1 to 3 (7, 7, and 6 minutes). The Case Study, Modern Example, Voices, Apply, and Level 4 pages are assigned for home. |
| Naming round | 10 | Gather question 4: each member reads the name on their Life Planner and the dark place on the second row of their Light Planner; one-sentence prayers for each. |

| **Total** | **75** | |

### ✅ Answer Key
**Q1.** The mother of Jesus was there, and Jesus and his disciples had been invited (John 2:1–2). John calls her 'the mother of Jesus' and never gives her name in his Gospel.

**Q2.** She says, "They have no wine" (John 2:3). His answer has a respectful but distancing question, "Woman, what have I to do with thee?" (John 2:4), and a statement: "mine hour is not yet come" (John 2:4).

**Q3.** She tells them, "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it" (John 2:5). They fill the jars to the brim, then draw out and carry to the governor, doing exactly what he says at each step (John 2:7–8).

**Q4.** Six waterpots, made of stone, set there for the Jews' purifying, each holding two or three firkins, which is roughly eighteen to twenty-seven gallons apiece if a firkin is about nine gallons (John 2:6).

**Q5.** He finds sellers of oxen, sheep, and doves and the money changers sitting; he makes a scourge of small cords; drives them all out with the sheep and oxen; pours out the changers' money; overturns the tables; and tells the dove sellers, "Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise" (John 2:14–16).

**Q6.** In verse 17 they remember Psalm 69:9, "The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up" (John 2:17); the text does not say whether this was at once or later. In verse 22, after he was risen from the dead, they remember his saying about the temple, and believe the scripture and his word (John 2:22).

**Q7.** Jesus is the Lord who comes suddenly to his temple to purify it (Malachi 3:1–3), consumed with zeal for God's house (Psalm 69:9), bringing the day when trade is gone from the house (Zechariah 14:21), hosting the promised feast (Isaiah 25:6), and in the end, with the Father, the temple of the city (Revelation 21:22). Worship now centres on him.

**Q8.** It points to Jesus as the one who fulfils and surpasses the old order of ceremonial purification: the water for washing becomes the wine of the feast, the joy of the promised age. The sign reveals his glory (John 2:11) and shows that "grace and truth came by Jesus Christ" (John 1:17).

**Q9.** They want proof that he has authority to act this way in the temple (John 2:18). He points them to the sign of his death and resurrection, which they themselves will bring about by destroying 'this temple', his body (John 2:19–21). It is the same sign he gives in the other Gospels, the sign of Jonas (Matthew 12:39–40).

**Q10.** The disciples saw his glory and "believed on him" (John 2:11), and they stayed with him. The many believed because they saw the signs, but Jesus did not entrust himself to them, because he knew their hearts (John 2:23–25); their faith rested on the signs, not yet on him, and faith like that often does not last (John 6:66).

**Q11.** Model answer, not the only answer: View B fits the way John uses 'hour' elsewhere, of the time of his death and glory (John 7:30; John 8:20; John 12:23; John 13:1; John 17:1). View A helps explain why Jesus then acts the same day. Many readers combine them: Jesus acts on the Father's timing, and every sign points ahead to the hour.

**Q12.** Both are grieved at the misuse of God's house and act to clear it (Nehemiah 13:8; John 2:15–17). Nehemiah could only clean a room; Jesus gives his own body as the new temple, destroyed and raised, and cleanses people, not just places (John 2:19–21; Hebrews 9:11).

**Q13.** Answers will vary. Point to the difference between believing "on him" (John 2:11) and believing because of what we see, and to Jesus' blessing on those "that have not seen, and yet have believed" (John 20:29).

**Q14.** Jesus measures what is happening in the temple not by its usefulness or custom but by the Father's claim on his house (John 2:16). That is the heart of the Confession's conviction that God appoints his own worship. Answers about drift will vary; direct the group to worship "in spirit and in truth" (John 4:24).

**Q15.** It proves he is the Son of God with authority over the temple and over death: "declared to be the Son of God with power... by the resurrection from the dead" (Romans 1:4). It turns the wine and the cleansing into signs of who he is, as the disciples saw after he rose (John 2:22).

**Q16.** Model answers: forgiving before feeling it, giving when the need is unclear, speaking of Christ when it feels awkward. The servants filled the jars "up to the brim" (John 2:7) before they saw anything happen.

**Q17.** Model answer: his zeal cost him his life; Psalm 69 reaches the cross, with vinegar for his thirst (Psalm 69:21; John 19:28–30). That turns us to gratitude and self-examination, not anger at others (John 2:17).

**Q18.** Model answers: putting away the phone during worship, giving without seeking recognition, confessing the wish to be seen, dropping a church activity that has crowded out prayer. Humbling ourselves means doing it quietly before God first (1 Peter 5:6; John 2:16).

**Q19.** Jesus seeks the Father's glory and his own true glory, not human applause; he says elsewhere, "I receive not honour from men" (John 5:41). His quietness at Cana rebukes our hunger for credit and frees us to serve unseen (John 2:9–10).

**Q20.** Model answers: a marriage that has gone flat, a friend in depression, a household after a loss, a church that has lost its first love. The wine has run out and only duty remains (John 2:3).

**Q21.** Model answers: joy, hope, trust, worship. The thief comes "to steal, and to kill, and to destroy" (John 10:10).

**Q22.** Christ gives himself: better wine than the first (John 2:10), and the risen temple where God is met (John 2:19). His gift is better because it cannot run out and does not depend on our circumstances: "that my joy might remain in you" (John 15:11).

**Q23.** Model answer: a coworker, a relative, a neighbour who does not know where the good things come from. The servants knew and the governor did not (John 2:9); a believer who knows should say so.

**Q24.** Model answers: a motive in service, a habit, a resentment, a fear. He already "knew what was in man" (John 2:25), so we can bring it to him openly and be cleansed (1 John 1:9).

**Q25.** Model answers: serving for recognition, giving for reputation, attending church for business contacts or social standing. Jesus' word is, "make not my Father's house an house of merchandise" (John 2:16), and he warns against doing good "to be seen of them" (Matthew 6:1).

**Q26.** Model answer: a friend who thinks Christianity is about buildings or rules; read John 2:19–22 with them, listen first, and explain gently that God is met in the risen Jesus. The Lord's servant must be "gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient" (2 Timothy 2:24).

### 🗺️ Life & Light Leader's Map
**Worked Life Planner Row:** *Who:* Ruth, my neighbour, widowed last spring. *What the thief has stolen:* her joy in ordinary things; she says the evenings are the worst. *What Christ gives instead:* better wine than the first, and a hope that does not run dry (John 2:10; John 11:25). *What I will do this week:* take her a meal on Thursday, stay to eat with her, and ask if I may pray with her. *Done?* A tick, and a note of what she said.

**Worked Light Planner Row:** *Where it is dark:* my own heart: I serve on the welcome team partly because I like being known as the helpful one. *What is hidden there:* the wish to be seen and thanked. *What light Christ shines:* he knows what is in man and still receives me (John 2:25), and he let the bridegroom take the praise at Cana (John 2:9–10). *How I carry it:* confess it to the Lord tonight, and this week do one task for the church that no one will know about. This first row stays private; in the naming round members read their second row.

**When Someone Has No One to Name:** Do not accept 'no one' too quickly, and do not shame the person either. Walk through their week with them: household, family, workplace or school, neighbours, the person they sit near on Sunday. Ask, 'Who in those places seems tired, lonely, or dry?' The servants at Cana did not choose the guests; they served whoever was at the feast. If they still cannot name anyone, suggest they ask the Lord for one name this week (Matthew 9:38).

**When Someone Points the Light at Others:** When a member uses the temple cleansing to talk about other people's worship, another church, or a family member's sins, bring them gently back to the first row of the Light Planner, their own heart. Remind the group that Jesus is the Lord of the house and we are not, that his zeal consumed himself and not others (John 2:17), and that the Love Guard is printed in the lesson for this reason. If there is a real concern about someone else, suggest the private, humble way of Matthew 18:15, after the plank has come out of their own eye (Matthew 7:5).

### 🐑 Shepherding Notes
This chapter touches several tender places. Handle them with care.

- **Alcohol.** For a member in recovery, or a family harmed by drinking, a story about Jesus making much wine can be painful. Acknowledge it plainly: the sign is about his glory, not a recommendation to drink, and Scripture honours those who abstain for a brother's sake (Romans 14:21). Do not let the group joke about the wine.
- **Weddings and marriage.** For singles who long to marry, the widowed, the divorced, and couples whose marriage has run dry, a wedding story may sting. The Bridegroom here is Christ, and every believer belongs to his feast (Revelation 19:9).
- **Mothers and sons.** 'Woman, what have I to do with thee?' may stir memories of broken family relationships. Point to John 19:26–27, where the same Jesus, in agony, provides for his mother.
- **Church hurt.** Some have been in churches that felt like markets: pressure to give, ministry for profit, leaders who used people. Jesus is against the misuse of his Father's house. Listen before you teach, and do not defend what should not be defended.
- **Faith built on excitement.** Some came to faith through dramatic experiences and now feel dry, or prayed for miracles that did not come. John 2:23–25 can frighten them. Reassure them that Jesus receives everyone who comes to him (John 6:37).
- **The Light Planner's first row.** It is private: never ask anyone to read it aloud, and say so at the start of the naming round. If someone chooses to share, receive it quietly, pray, and keep it in the group.

### 🎯 Teaching Angles
**For a Tier 1 Group:** Tell the two stories as stories. Bring a bucket and a cup to show how much water the servants carried. Ask: What did Jesus do? What did it show about him? What did the servants have to do? Finish with the promise that he rose from the dead just as he said. Use the Tier 1 section.

**For a Tier 2 Group:** Trace two lines. The temple line: the tabernacle (Exodus 25:8), Jesus' body (John 2:21), the church (1 Corinthians 3:16), the city with no temple (Revelation 21:22). The hour line: John 2:4, John 7:30, John 12:23, John 17:1. Then read the two scenes as one message: Jesus replaces the water of purification and the temple of stone with himself.

**Tough Question 1:** *Did Jesus make alcoholic wine, and does that mean Christians should drink?* The ordinary word for wine is used, and the governor's remark assumes real wine; it is the most natural reading. That shows wine is not evil in itself (Psalm 104:15). It does not command anyone to drink. Scripture condemns drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18), and a believer may abstain for the sake of others (Romans 14:21). Both the drinker and the abstainer must not judge the other, and both must keep the focus on the sign: the glory of Christ.

**Tough Question 2:** *Was Jesus angry, and wasn't the whip violent?* He was zealous, and zeal can include holy anger at the misuse of God's house (John 2:17). But he acted as Lord of the temple fulfilling prophecy (Malachi 3:1), not as a private man settling a grudge. The whip may have been used only on the animals, and no one is said to have been hurt. This gives no licence for violence in God's name; his zeal ended with himself consumed on the cross.

**Tough Question 3:** *If the people in John 2:23 'believed in his name', were they saved, and how can I know my own faith is real?* John does not say what finally became of them; he says their faith rested on signs and Jesus did not entrust himself to it (John 2:24–25). For our own assurance, the answer is to look at Christ, not at the strength of our faith: "him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out" (John 6:37). Real faith keeps coming to him and continues in his word (John 8:31), and the fruit of that is seen over time, not in a single moment.
